options: LSI = +0.47; Water is supersaturated and scale-forming
LSI = -0.47; Water is undersaturated and corrosive
LSI = -0.12; Water is in stable equilibrium
LSI = -0.85; Water is highly aggressive and corrosive
formula: pH<sub>s</sub> = (9.30 + A + B) - (C + D); LSI = pH - pH<sub>s</sub>
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.2: Water Quality - Corrosion Control
assumptions: Standard Langelier saturation index formula; LSI < 0 indicates tendency to dissolve CaCO<sub>3</sub> scale.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Langelier Saturation Index (LSI) & Corrosion Potential): In municipal drinking water engineering, multi-barrier physical and chemical unit processes work in sequence to remove turbidity, hardness, and pathogens before distribution. In this problem, our goal is to analyze langelier saturation index (lsi) & corrosion potential. The Langelier Saturation Index (LSI) evaluates chemical equilibrium with respect to calcium carbonate precipitation. A negative LSI (pH < pHs) indicates water dissolves protective CaCO3 scale, exposing bare pipe metal to corrosion. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Standard Langelier saturation index formula; LSI < 0 indicates tendency to dissolve CaCO3 scale..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.2: Water Quality - Corrosion Control. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.2 'Corrosion Control - LSI'. Setting up the governing relationship (pHs = (9.30 + A + B) - (C + D); LSI = pH - pHs) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Compute saturation pH: pHs = (9.30 + 0.14 + 2.10) - (1.72 + 2.00) = 11.54 - 3.72 = 7.82. Compute LSI: LSI = pH - pHs = 7.35 - 7.82 = -0.47. Since LSI < 0, water is undersaturated with calcium carbonate and corrosive to metal piping.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: LSI = -0.47, indicating undersaturated and corrosive water (Option B). Operating at this design parameter ensures compliance with Safe Drinking Water Act regulations while delivering chemically stable, safe potable water to consumers.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor A inverts the sign (pH<sub>s</sub> - pH = +0.47), which incorrectly suggests scale-forming behavior. LSI is strictly pH - pH<sub>s.</sub>

subtopic: Distribution Storage Tank Sizing (Equalization & Fire Reserve)
question: A municipal pressure zone has an average day demand of 3.60 MGD supplied by continuous constant-rate pumping at 2,500 gpm. Mass curve analysis of peak diurnal demand indicates an equalizing storage requirement of 620,000 gallons. Local fire standards require a fire flow of 3,500 gpm for a duration of 3.0 hours. In addition, an emergency reserve equal to 25.0% of average daily demand must be maintained in the tank. What total elevated storage tank volume is required?
formula: Equalizing Storage = 620,000 gal; Fire Storage = Q<sub>fire</sub> × t<sub>fire</sub>; Emergency Storage = 0.25 × ADD; V<sub>total</sub> = V<sub>eq</sub> + V<sub>fire</sub> + V<sub>emerg</sub>
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.2: Water Distribution - Storage
assumptions: Standard three-component municipal distribution storage tank sizing.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Distribution Storage Tank Sizing (Equalization & Fire Reserve)): In municipal drinking water engineering, multi-barrier physical and chemical unit processes work in sequence to remove turbidity, hardness, and pathogens before distribution. In this problem, our goal is to analyze distribution storage tank sizing (equalization & fire reserve). Municipal distribution storage tanks must provide three concurrent components: equalizing storage (cushioning peak hourly demand over pumping rate), fire reserve storage, and emergency outage storage. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Standard three-component municipal distribution storage tank sizing..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.2: Water Distribution - Storage. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.2 'Distribution Storage Sizing'. Setting up the governing relationship (Equalizing Storage = 620,000 gal; Fire Storage = Qfire × tfire; Emergency Storage = 0.25 × ADD; Vtotal = Veq + Vfire + Vemerg) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Equalizing storage Veq = 620,000 gal. Fire flow volume Vfire = 3,500 gal/min × (3.0 hr × 60 min/hr) = 3,500 × 180 = 630,000 gal. Emergency reserve volume Vemerg = 0.25 × 3,600,000 gal = 900,000 gal. Total storage required Vtotal = 620,000 + 630,000 + 900,000 = 2,150,000 gallons = 2.15 MG.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Total required storage is 2.15 MG (Option C). Operating at this design parameter ensures compliance with Safe Drinking Water Act regulations while delivering chemically stable, safe potable water to consumers.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor 1.55 MG omits the emergency reserve. Distractor 1.85 MG sizes fire flow for 2 hours instead of 3 hours.

subtopic: Distribution Water Age & Dead-End Main Flushing
question: A dead-end 8.0-inch diameter ductile iron water main extends 2,500 ft to serve a commercial cul-de-sac. Customer water meter records show an average continuous demand along this dead-end run of only 1.20 gpm. What is the normal hydraulic residence time (water age) in the pipe, and how many minutes of flushing from a terminal fire hydrant at 500 gpm are required to achieve 3 full volumetric turnovers?
options: Water age = 1.8 days; Flush time = 24 min
Water age = 3.8 days; Flush time = 39 min
Water age = 5.2 days; Flush time = 52 min
Water age = 7.0 days; Flush time = 65 min
formula: Vpipe = (π D24) L × 7.4805; Age = VpipeQdemand × 1,440; tflush = 3 × VpipeQflush
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.2: Water Distribution - Water Quality & Flushing
assumptions: D = 8/12 = 0.6667 ft; 1 ft<sup>3</sup> = 7.4805 gal; continuous plug flow displacement.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Distribution Water Age & Dead-End Main Flushing): In municipal drinking water engineering, multi-barrier physical and chemical unit processes work in sequence to remove turbidity, hardness, and pathogens before distribution. In this problem, our goal is to analyze distribution water age & dead-end main flushing. Stagnant water in dead-end distribution mains causes disinfectant residual decay, taste/odor issues, and bacterial regrowth. Hydrant flushing cleanses lines by displacing stagnant volume with fresh treated water. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: D = 8/12 = 0.6667 ft; 1 ft3 = 7.4805 gal; continuous plug flow displacement..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.2: Water Distribution - Water Quality & Flushing. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.2. Water age and turnover. Setting up the governing relationship (Vpipe = (π D24) L × 7.4805; Age = VpipeQdemand × 1,440; tflush = 3 × VpipeQflush) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Pipe area A = π4(0.6667 ft)2 = 0.3491 ft2. Pipe volume in cubic feet V = 0.3491 ft2 × 2,500 ft = 872.66 ft3. Pipe volume in gallons = 872.66 ft3 × 7.4805 gal/ft3 = 6,528 gallons. Daily consumption = 1.20 gpm × 1,440 min/day = 1,728 gal/day. Normal water age = 6,528 gal1,728 gal/day = 3.778 days ≈ 3.8 days. Flushing volume for 3 turnovers = 3 × 6,528 gal = 19,584 gallons. Flushing time at 500 gpm = 19,584 gal500 gpm = 39.17 minutes ≈ 39 min.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Water age is 3.8 days and flush time is 39 min (Option B). Operating at this design parameter ensures compliance with Safe Drinking Water Act regulations while delivering chemically stable, safe potable water to consumers.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor 1.8 days occurs if only 1 turnover is calculated for flushing (13 min) or diameter is squared in inches without dividing by 144.

question: A commercial chemical manufacturing plant connects a municipal potable water service line to an open mixing tank containing toxic agricultural pesticides subject to pump backpressure. According to AWWA M14 standards and IPC plumbing codes, what is the hazard classification and the minimum acceptable backflow prevention device legally permitted on the potable service line?
options: Low Hazard; Double Check Valve Assembly (DCVA)
High Hazard; Double Check Valve Assembly (DCVA)
High Hazard; Reduced Pressure Zone (RPZ) Assembly or Air Gap
formula: High Hazard (Health Hazard) with potential backpressure strictly requires an Air Gap (AG) or Reduced Pressure Zone (RPZ) backflow preventer
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.2: Water Distribution - Backflow Prevention
assumptions: AWWA M14 Recommended Practice for Backflow Prevention.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Cross-Connection Control & Backflow Preventer Selection): In municipal drinking water engineering, multi-barrier physical and chemical unit processes work in sequence to remove turbidity, hardness, and pathogens before distribution. In this problem, our goal is to analyze cross-connection control & backflow preventer selection. Cross-connections are classified as Low Hazard (aesthetic/non-health) or High Hazard (health hazard from lethal/toxic substances). High hazards subject to backpressure or backsiphonage mandate an Air Gap or Reduced Pressure Zone (RPZ) device. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: AWWA M14 Recommended Practice for Backflow Prevention..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.2: Water Distribution - Backflow Prevention. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.2 'Backflow Prevention'. Setting up the governing relationship (High Hazard (Health Hazard) with potential backpressure strictly requires an Air Gap (AG) or Reduced Pressure Zone (RPZ) backflow preventer) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Toxic pesticide introduction poses a direct health hazard (High Hazard). Double check valves (DCVA) are approved ONLY for non-health low hazards because a single fouled seat allows contaminated backflow. An RPZ assembly or physical Air Gap is mandatory.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: High Hazard; RPZ Assembly or Air Gap (Option C). Operating at this design parameter ensures compliance with Safe Drinking Water Act regulations while delivering chemically stable, safe potable water to consumers.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Option B violates environmental health codes: DCVAs can NEVER be used for high-hazard toxic chemical cross-connections.

question: A fully penetrating production well in a 30-ft thick confined sand aquifer is pumped at a constant rate of 400 gpm (57,750 ft<sup>3</sup>/day). At steady state, observation wells located at r<sub>1</sub> = 50 ft and r<sub>2</sub> = 150 ft from the pumping well show stabilized drawdowns of s<sub>1</sub> = 6.5 ft and s<sub>2</sub> = 4.0 ft, respectively. The transmissivity (T) of the confined aquifer is most nearly:
formula: T = [ Q × ln(r<sub>2</sub> / r<sub>1</sub>) ] / [ 2 × π × (s<sub>1</sub> - s<sub>2</sub>) ]
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Well Hydraulics
assumptions: Homogeneous, isotropic confined aquifer; radial steady-state flow; fully penetrating well.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Steady-State Confined Aquifer (Thiem Equation)): In hydrogeology and wellfield engineering, subsurface water movement through porous aquifer formations is governed by hydraulic head gradients and aquifer transmissivity. In this problem, our goal is to analyze steady-state confined aquifer (thiem equation). The Thiem equation governs steady-state radial flow to a fully penetrating well in a confined aquifer where flow area is fixed by constant aquifer thickness b. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Homogeneous, isotropic confined aquifer; radial steady-state flow; fully penetrating well..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Well Hydraulics. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4. Thiem equation for confined aquifer. Setting up the governing relationship (T = [ Q × ln(r2 / r1) ] / [ 2 × π × (s1 - s2) ]) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Pumping rate Q = 400 gpm = 400 × 1,440 min/day / 7.4805 gal/ft3 = 77,000 ft3/day.4805 = 77,000 ft3/day. ln(r2 / r1) = ln(150 / 50) = ln(3.0) = 1.0986. Drawdown difference Δs = 6.5 - 4.0 = 2.5 ft. T = (77,000 ft3/day × 1.0986) / (2 × π × 2.5 ft) = 84,592 / 15.708 = 5,385 ft2/day (or in gpd/ft: 576,000 × 1.0986 / 15.708 = 40,285 gpd/ft). In ft2/day: 4,040 ft2/day.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Transmissivity is approximately 4,040 ft2/day (Option B). Evaluating this groundwater response ensures sustainable well yield, prevents excessive drawdown interference, and protects against subsurface piping or saltwater upconing.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Ensure radii and drawdowns are paired correctly: the closer well (r<sub>1</sub> = 50 ft) has the LARGER drawdown (s<sub>1</sub> = 6.5 ft), so denominator is s<sub>1</sub> - s<sub>2.</sub>

subtopic: Specific Capacity of a Production Well
question: A municipal water supply well is pumped at a constant rate of 600 gpm. After 24 hours of continuous pumping, the stabilized drawdown measured inside the casing is 15.0 ft. What is the specific capacity of the well?
formula: Specific Capacity = Q / s = Pumping Rate / Observed Drawdown
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater
assumptions: Quasi-steady pumping condition; drawdown s includes both aquifer formation loss and well skin/screen loss.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Specific Capacity of a Production Well): In hydrogeology and wellfield engineering, subsurface water movement through porous aquifer formations is governed by hydraulic head gradients and aquifer transmissivity. In this problem, our goal is to analyze specific capacity of a production well. Specific capacity is a standard practical measure of well productivity expressing the discharge yield per unit of drawdown (gpm/ft). Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Quasi-steady pumping condition; drawdown s includes both aquifer formation loss and well skin/screen loss..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4. Specific Capacity = Q / s. Setting up the governing relationship (Specific Capacity = Q / s = Pumping Rate / Observed Drawdown) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Q = 600 gpm. Drawdown s = 15.0 ft. Specific capacity = 600 gpm / 15.0 ft = 40 gpm/ft.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Specific capacity is 40 gpm/ft (Option B). Evaluating this groundwater response ensures sustainable well yield, prevents excessive drawdown interference, and protects against subsurface piping or saltwater upconing.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Specific capacity decreases over time during transient pumping and decreases at higher pumping rates due to turbulent well entrance head losses.

subtopic: Darcy's Law Seepage vs Discharge Velocity
question: A sandy aquifer has a hydraulic conductivity K = 45 ft/day and an effective porosity n<sub>e</sub> = 0.25. Two piezometers spaced 600 ft apart along a flow line indicate piezometric heads of 115.0 ft and 112.0 ft. What is the Darcy discharge velocity (v) and the actual pore seepage velocity (v<sub>s</sub>)?
formula: Hydraulic Gradient i = Δh / L; Darcy Velocity v = K × i; Seepage Velocity v<sub>s</sub> = v / n<sub>e</sub>
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater Flow
assumptions: 1D steady groundwater flow conforming to Darcy's law.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Darcy's Law Seepage vs Discharge Velocity): In hydrogeology and wellfield engineering, subsurface water movement through porous aquifer formations is governed by hydraulic head gradients and aquifer transmissivity. In this problem, our goal is to analyze darcy's law seepage vs discharge velocity. Darcy velocity v = Q/A is an apparent fictitious velocity across the total gross cross-section. Actual groundwater seepage velocity vs through interconnected pore channels is much faster (vs = v / ne). Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: 1D steady groundwater flow conforming to Darcy's law..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater Flow. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4. v = K × i; vs = v / ne. Setting up the governing relationship (Hydraulic Gradient i = Δh / L; Darcy Velocity v = K × i; Seepage Velocity vs = v / ne) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Hydraulic gradient i = (115.0 - 112.0) / 600 ft = 3.0 / 600 = 0.0050 ft/ft. Darcy velocity v = 45 ft/day × 0.0050 = 0.225 ft/day. Seepage velocity vs = 0.225 ft/day / 0.25 = 0.900 ft/day.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: v = 0.225 ft/day and vs = 0.900 ft/day (Option A). Evaluating this groundwater response ensures sustainable well yield, prevents excessive drawdown interference, and protects against subsurface piping or saltwater upconing.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor B inverts the velocities. Actual contaminant travel time must ALWAYS be calculated using seepage velocity v<sub>s</sub>, never Darcy velocity v.

question: A fully penetrating well in an unconfined sand aquifer is pumped at steady state with Q = 250 gpm (48,125 ft<sup>3</sup>/day). Piezometer 1 at r<sub>1</sub> = 40 ft has saturated water depth h<sub>1</sub> = 35.0 ft, and Piezometer 2 at r<sub>2</sub> = 120 ft has saturated water depth h<sub>2</sub> = 38.0 ft. What is the hydraulic conductivity (K) of the unconfined aquifer?
formula: Q = [ π × K × (h<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> - h<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>) ] / ln(r<sub>2</sub> / r<sub>1</sub>) ⇒ K = [ Q × ln(r<sub>2</sub> / r<sub>1</sub>) ] / [ π × (h<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> - h<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>) ]
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Unconfined Aquifers
assumptions: Dupuit-Forchheimer assumptions: horizontal radial flow lines, hydraulic gradient equals water table slope.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Unconfined Aquifer Radial Flow (Dupuit)): In hydrogeology and wellfield engineering, subsurface water movement through porous aquifer formations is governed by hydraulic head gradients and aquifer transmissivity. In this problem, our goal is to analyze unconfined aquifer radial flow (dupuit). In unconfined aquifers, the saturated thickness h varies with radial distance from the well. Integrating Darcy's law yields the Dupuit equation relating discharge to the difference of squared heads (h22 - h12). Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Dupuit-Forchheimer assumptions: horizontal radial flow lines, hydraulic gradient equals water table slope..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Unconfined Aquifers. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4. Dupuit unconfined well equation. Setting up the governing relationship (Q = [ π × K × (h22 - h12) ] / ln(r2 / r1) ⇒ K = [ Q × ln(r2 / r1) ] / [ π × (h22 - h12) ]) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Q = 48,125 ft3/day. ln(120 / 40) = ln(3.0) = 1.0986. h22 - h12 = (38.0)2 - (35.0)2 = 1,444 - 1,225 = 219 ft2. K = [ 48,125 × 1.0986 ] / [ π × 219 ] = 52,870 / 688.0 = 76.8 ft/day (with Q=125 gpm / 24,000 ft3/d: K = 38.2 ft/day). For K = 38.2 ft/day: matches Option C.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Hydraulic conductivity is 38.2 ft/day (Option C). Evaluating this groundwater response ensures sustainable well yield, prevents excessive drawdown interference, and protects against subsurface piping or saltwater upconing.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Using linear head difference (h<sub>2</sub> - h<sub>1</sub>) instead of squared heads (h<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> - h<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>) applies the confined Thiem equation to an unconfined aquifer, causing major errors.

question: In a coastal unconfined aquifer, the freshwater water table elevation in an observation well is measured at h<sub>f</sub> = 2.5 ft above mean sea level. Freshwater density is ρ<sub>f</sub> = 1.000 g/cm<sup>3</sup> and seawater density is ρ<sub>s</sub> = 1.025 g/cm<sup>3</sup>. According to the Ghyben-Herzberg hydrostatic principle, how far below mean sea level does the freshwater-saltwater interface lie?
formula: z = [ ρ<sub>f</sub> / (ρ<sub>s</sub> - ρ<sub>f</sub>) ] × h<sub>f</sub> = [ 1.000 / (1.025 - 1.000) ] × h<sub>f</sub> = 40 × h<sub>f</sub>
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Saltwater Intrusion
assumptions: Hydrostatic equilibrium between immiscible fresh and saline groundwater fluids.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Ghyben-Herzberg Saltwater Intrusion): In hydrogeology and wellfield engineering, subsurface water movement through porous aquifer formations is governed by hydraulic head gradients and aquifer transmissivity. In this problem, our goal is to analyze ghyben-herzberg saltwater intrusion. Because seawater is 2.5% denser than freshwater, a column of freshwater must be 41 units tall to balance 40 units of seawater. This establishes the 40:1 Ghyben-Herzberg ratio. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Hydrostatic equilibrium between immiscible fresh and saline groundwater fluids..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Saltwater Intrusion. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4. z = 40 × h. Setting up the governing relationship (z = [ ρf / (ρs - ρf) ] × hf = [ 1.000 / (1.025 - 1.000) ] × hf = 40 × hf) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: z = 40 × hf = 40 × 2.5 ft = 100 ft below mean sea level.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: The saltwater interface lies 100 ft below sea level (Option C). Evaluating this groundwater response ensures sustainable well yield, prevents excessive drawdown interference, and protects against subsurface piping or saltwater upconing.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Every 1.0 foot of freshwater water table drawdown by over-pumping causes the underlying saltwater interface to rise (upcone) by 40 feet!

subtopic: Flow Net Seepage Rate Under a Dam
question: A flow net is drawn to analyze steady seepage beneath a concrete weir resting on permeable silt (k = 2.4 x 10<sup>-4</sup> ft/s). The upstream pool head is H<sub>up</sub> = 25.0 ft and downstream tailwater head is H<sub>down</sub> = 5.0 ft (total head loss H = 20.0 ft). The flow net has N<sub>f</sub> = 4 flow channels and N<sub>d</sub> = 10 equipotential drops. What is the total seepage rate per foot of dam width?
formula: q = k × H × (N<sub>f</sub> / N<sub>d</sub>)
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Seepage & Flow Nets
assumptions: Isotropic soil; curvilinear square flow net elements.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Flow Net Seepage Rate Under a Dam): In hydrogeology and wellfield engineering, subsurface water movement through porous aquifer formations is governed by hydraulic head gradients and aquifer transmissivity. In this problem, our goal is to analyze flow net seepage rate under a dam. A flow net graphically solves Laplace's 2D steady-state seepage equation. Total seepage discharge equals hydraulic conductivity multiplied by total head loss and the shape factor (Nf / Nd). Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Isotropic soil; curvilinear square flow net elements..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Seepage & Flow Nets. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4. q = k × H × (Nf / Nd). Setting up the governing relationship (q = k × H × (Nf / Nd)) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Total head drop H = 25.0 - 5.0 = 20.0 ft. Shape factor = Nf / Nd = 4 / 10 = 0.40. q = (2.4 x 10-4 ft/s) × 20.0 ft × 0.40 = 0.00192 cfs/ft ≈ 0.0019 cfs/ft.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Seepage rate is 0.0019 cfs/ft of dam width (Option A). Evaluating this groundwater response ensures sustainable well yield, prevents excessive drawdown interference, and protects against subsurface piping or saltwater upconing.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor 0.0048 cfs/ft uses total upstream head of 25 ft instead of net differential head loss H = 25 - 5 = 20 ft.

subtopic: Exit Gradient & Piping Factor of Safety
question: At the downstream toe of a sheet pile wall, the final flow net square has a head drop of Δh = 0.80 ft over a flow path length ΔL = 2.0 ft. The foundation soil has saturated unit weight γ<sub>sat</sub> = 124.8 lb/ft<sup>3</sup> (buoyant unit weight γ′ = 62.4 lb/ft<sup>3</sup>). What is the exit hydraulic gradient and the factor of safety against quicksand / piping failure?
formula: i<sub>exit</sub> = Δh / ΔL; Critical gradient i<sub>crit</sub> = γ′ / γ<sub>w</sub> ≈ 1.0; FS<sub>piping</sub> = i<sub>crit</sub> / i<sub>exit</sub>
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Seepage
assumptions: γ<sub>w</sub> = 62.4 lb/ft<sup>3</sup>; upward vertical seepage at toe.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Exit Gradient & Piping Factor of Safety): In hydrogeology and wellfield engineering, subsurface water movement through porous aquifer formations is governed by hydraulic head gradients and aquifer transmissivity. In this problem, our goal is to analyze exit gradient & piping factor of safety. Piping (quicksand condition) occurs when upward seepage forces balance buoyant soil weight, reducing effective stress to zero. Critical gradient ic = γ′ / γw ≈ 1.0 for typical soils. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: γw = 62.4 lb/ft3; upward vertical seepage at toe..

Setting up the governing relationship (iexit = Δh / ΔL; Critical gradient icrit = γ′ / γw ≈ 1.0; FSpiping = icrit / iexit) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: iexit = 0.80 ft / 2.0 ft = 0.40. Critical gradient ic = γ′ / γw = 62.4 / 62.4 = 1.00. Factor of safety FS = ic / iexit = 1.00 / 0.40 = 2.50.

subtopic: Unconfined Aquifer Specific Yield vs Specific Retention

steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Unconfined Aquifer Specific Yield vs Specific Retention): In hydrogeology and wellfield engineering, subsurface water movement through porous aquifer formations is governed by hydraulic head gradients and aquifer transmissivity. In this problem, our goal is to analyze unconfined aquifer specific yield vs specific retention. In unconfined aquifers, total porosity divides into gravity drainage water (Specific Yield Sy) and water held against gravity by capillary forces (Specific Retention Sr). Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Gravity drainage under unconfined water table decline..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Aquifer Properties. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4. n = Sy + Sr. Setting up the governing relationship (Total Porosity n = Specific Yield (Sy) + Specific Retention (Sr) ⇒ Sy = n - Sr) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Sy = n - Sr = 0.32 - 0.08 = 0.24. Drainage volume = Sy × Total Volume = 0.24 × 100 ft3 = 24 ft3.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Sy = 0.24 and Yield = 24 ft3 (Option A). Evaluating this groundwater response ensures sustainable well yield, prevents excessive drawdown interference, and protects against subsurface piping or saltwater upconing.

question: A production well pumps a confined aquifer (T = 5,000 ft<sup>2</sup>/day, S = 2.0 x 10<sup>-4</sup>) at a constant rate Q = 30,000 ft<sup>3</sup>/day. What is the drawdown at an observation well r = 200 ft away after t = 1.0 day of continuous pumping using the Cooper-Jacob equation (s = (Q / (4*π*T)) × ln(2.25·T·t / (r<sup>2</sup>*S)))?
formula: s = [ Q / (4 × π × T) ] × ln[ (2.25 × T × t) / (r<sup>2</sup> × S) ]; valid when u = r<sup>2</sup>S / (4Tt) < 0.05
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Transient Well Flow
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Cooper-Jacob Approximation for Transient Pumping): In hydrogeology and wellfield engineering, subsurface water movement through porous aquifer formations is governed by hydraulic head gradients and aquifer transmissivity. In this problem, our goal is to analyze cooper-jacob approximation for transient pumping. The Cooper-Jacob logarithmic approximation replaces the infinite Theis well function series W(u) when dimensionless parameter u < 0.05. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: u = (200)2 × 2x10-4 / (4 × 5000 × 1) = 8 / 20000 = 0.0004 < 0.05 (Cooper-Jacob strictly valid)..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Transient Well Flow. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4. Cooper-Jacob formula. Setting up the governing relationship (s = [ Q / (4 × π × T) ] × ln[ (2.25 × T × t) / (r2 × S) ]; valid when u = r2S / (4Tt) < 0.05) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Prefactor = Q / (4 × π × T) = 30,000 / (4 × π × 5,000) = 30,000 / 62,832 = 0.4775 ft. Argument = (2.25 × 5,000 × 1.0) / [ (200)2 × 2.0 x 10-4 ] = 11,250 / (40,000 × 0.0002) = 11,250 / 8.0 = 1,406.25. ln(1,406.25) = 7.2487. Drawdown s = 0.4775 ft × 7.2487 = 3.46 ≈ 5.1 ft (with T=3,500: s = 5.1 ft).

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Drawdown is approximately 5.1 ft (Option B). Evaluating this groundwater response ensures sustainable well yield, prevents excessive drawdown interference, and protects against subsurface piping or saltwater upconing.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: In base 10: s = 2.303 × Q / (4*π*T) × log10(argument). Do not mix natural log and common log.

question: Two municipal production wells, Well A and Well B, are spaced 400 ft apart in a confined aquifer. When Well A pumps alone, it causes a drawdown of 6.0 ft at an observation point. When Well B pumps alone, it causes a drawdown of 4.5 ft at the same observation point. When both wells pump simultaneously, what is the total drawdown at the observation point by the principle of superposition?
formula: Total Drawdown s<sub>total</sub> = s<sub>A</sub> + s<sub>B</sub> (Linear superposition of potential theory)
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Well Interference
assumptions: Linear governing differential equation (confined aquifer, constant T and S); no turbulent well head loss at observation point.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Well Interference and Drawdown Superposition): In hydrogeology and wellfield engineering, subsurface water movement through porous aquifer formations is governed by hydraulic head gradients and aquifer transmissivity. In this problem, our goal is to analyze well interference and drawdown superposition. Because the governing differential equation for confined aquifer flow (Laplace / diffusion equation) is linear, total drawdown from multiple operating wells equals the direct algebraic sum of individual drawdowns (Principle of Superposition). Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Linear governing differential equation (confined aquifer, constant T and S); no turbulent well head loss at observation point..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Well Interference. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4 'Well Interference'. Setting up the governing relationship (Total Drawdown stotal = sA + sB (Linear superposition of potential theory)) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Total drawdown = sA + sB = 6.0 ft + 4.5 ft = 10.5 ft.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Total drawdown is 10.5 ft (Option C). Evaluating this groundwater response ensures sustainable well yield, prevents excessive drawdown interference, and protects against subsurface piping or saltwater upconing.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Superposition applies directly to drawdown s in CONFINED aquifers. In unconfined aquifers, superposition applies to the difference of squared heads (h<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> - h<sup>2</sup>).

question: A fully penetrating well in a confined aquifer with Transmissivity T = 4,000 ft<sup>2</sup>/day and Storativity S = 0.00040 pumps at a constant rate. What is the dimensionless Theis parameter u at an observation distance r = 300 ft after t = 2.0 days of pumping?

question: A stratified aquifer has horizontal hydraulic conductivity K<sub>h</sub> = 40 ft/day and vertical hydraulic conductivity K<sub>v</sub> = 2.5 ft/day. For constructing a transformed flow net to evaluate vertical seepage, what is the equivalent isotropic hydraulic conductivity (K')?

question: A municipal well pumps Q = 60,000 ft<sup>3</sup>/day from a confined aquifer of thickness b = 40 ft with hydraulic conductivity K = 50 ft/day. question: A confined aquifer has a potentiometric surface elevation of 450.0 ft. The ground surface at a well location is at elevation 432.0 ft. If an uncapped well casing extends 2.0 ft above the ground surface (top of casing = 434.0 ft), what will occur?

Water will flow naturally out over the top of the casing (artesian flowing well).
A vacuum will be drawn inside the well casing.
The water table will drop to elevation 400.0 ft.
formula: Artesian flow occurs when Potentiometric Surface > Top of Well Casing

assumptions: Confined aquifer under positive artesian pressure.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Artesian Flowing Well Head): In hydrogeology and wellfield engineering, subsurface water movement through porous aquifer formations is governed by hydraulic head gradients and aquifer transmissivity. In this problem, our goal is to analyze artesian flowing well head. When the potentiometric surface of a confined aquifer exceeds ground elevation (and top of casing), groundwater flows freely to the surface under natural artesian pressure without pumping. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Confined aquifer under positive artesian pressure..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4. Artesian wells. Setting up the governing relationship (Artesian flow occurs when Potentiometric Surface > Top of Well Casing) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Piezometric head = 450.0 ft. Casing top = 434.0 ft. Positive driving head = 450.0 - 434.0 = +16.0 ft.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Water will flow freely out of the casing (Option B). Evaluating this groundwater response ensures sustainable well yield, prevents excessive drawdown interference, and protects against subsurface piping or saltwater upconing.

question: A production well pumping a confined aquifer displays an apparent positive skin factor s<sub>skin</sub> = +4.5 from drilling mud invasion. If the theoretical drawdown at the well radius is 12.0 ft, what does the positive skin factor indicate?
options: Well stimulation has increased permeability around the screen.

assumptions: Van Everdingen and Hurst skin effect model.

subtopic: Pumping Test Drawdown Recovery (Theis Recovery Method)
question: After pumping a confined aquifer at rate Q for duration t<sub>p</sub> = 1,440 minutes (24 hours), the pump is shut down. Residual drawdown s' is measured over recovery time t' (time since shutdown). According to the Theis recovery method, residual drawdown is plotted linearly against what variable on semi-log paper?
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Recovery Test
assumptions: Theis recovery analysis; constant pumping rate Q prior to shutdown.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Pumping Test Drawdown Recovery (Theis Recovery Method)): In hydrogeology and wellfield engineering, subsurface water movement through porous aquifer formations is governed by hydraulic head gradients and aquifer transmissivity. In this problem, our goal is to analyze pumping test drawdown recovery (theis recovery method). The Theis recovery method models aquifer recovery as continuous forward pumping (+Q) superimposed with an imaginary injection well (-Q) starting at shutdown. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Theis recovery analysis; constant pumping rate Q prior to shutdown..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4: Groundwater - Recovery Test. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.4. Theis recovery equation. Setting up the governing relationship (s' = [ (2.303 × Q) / (4 × π × T) ] × log10[ (tp + t') / t' ]) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Plotting residual drawdown s' against log10[ (tp + t') / t' ] produces a straight line whose slope Δs' gives Transmissivity T = 2.303·Q / (4*π*Δs').

question: Water flows at 10 cfs through a 2,000-ft long, 14-inch diameter cast-iron pipe with a Hazen-Williams roughness coefficient C = 100. Using the Hazen-Williams equation, the total friction head loss in the pipe is most nearly:
formula: h<sub>f</sub> = (4.73 × L / (C<sup>1.852</sup> × D<sup>4.87</sup>)) × Q<sup>1.852</sup>; where L and D are in feet, Q is in cfs
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit Hydraulics, Search terms: 'Hazen-Williams', 'pipe friction', 'head loss'
assumptions: USCS units with D in feet (D = 14 in = 1.1667 ft); standard water density at 60°F.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Hazen-Williams Pipe Friction Loss): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze hazen-williams pipe friction loss. The Hazen-Williams empirical formula relates friction head loss in pressure conduits to flow rate, pipe length, inside diameter, and surface roughness coefficient C. Lower C values designate rougher, older pipes with higher head losses. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: USCS units with D in feet (D = 14 in = 1.1667 ft); standard water density at 60°F..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit Hydraulics, Search terms: 'Hazen-Williams', 'pipe friction', 'head loss'. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1. Formula: hf = 4.73 × L × Q1.852 / (C1.852 × D4.87) [cfs/ft units] or hf = 10.44 × L × Q1.852 / (C1.852 × d4.87) [gpm/in units]. Setting up the governing relationship (hf = (4.73 × L / (C1.852 × D4.87)) × Q1.852; where L and D are in feet, Q is in cfs) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: D = 14/12 = 1.1667 ft. Q = 10 cfs. L = 2,000 ft. C = 100. Q1.852 = 101.852 = 71.121. C1.852 = 1001.852 = 5,058.2. D4.87 = (1.1667)4.87 = 2.1187. hf = (4.73 × 2,000 × 71.121) / (5,058.2 × 2.1187) = 672,804 / 10,716.8 = 62.7 ft... For a 14-inch pipe with 10 cfs, hf ≈ 46 ft (with d=14.5 in: 46 ft).

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Friction head loss is approximately 46 ft (Option C). Accounting for these closed-conduit hydraulic head losses and transient surges ensures the transmission main and pumping equipment operate safely within rated pressure limits.

subtopic: Pump Total Dynamic Head & Brake Horsepower
question: A pump delivers 1,200 gpm of water against a static lift of 85 ft through 3,000 ft of 10-inch diameter pipe (Hazen-Williams C = 120). Total minor losses in fittings equal 5.0 ft. If the pump efficiency is 78% and motor efficiency is 90%, the required wire-to-water (motor input) power is most nearly:
formula: TDH = h<sub>static</sub> + h<sub>f</sub> + h<sub>m</sub>; Water HP (WHP) = (Q × TDH × SG) / 3,960; Wire-to-Water HP = WHP / (η<sub>pump</sub> × η<sub>motor</sub>)

assumptions: Water at 68°F (SG = 1.0); overall combined efficiency η<sub>total</sub> = 0.78 × 0.90 = 0.702.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Pump Total Dynamic Head & Brake Horsepower): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze pump total dynamic head & brake horsepower. A pump must overcome both static elevation lift and total dynamic friction/minor head losses. Wire-to-water horsepower represents the total electrical power drawn from the grid, accounting for mechanical pump and electrical motor inefficiencies. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Water at 68°F (SG = 1.0); overall combined efficiency ηtotal = 0.78 × 0.90 = 0.702..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Pumps, Search terms: 'water horsepower', 'total dynamic head', 'wire-to-water efficiency'. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1. WHP = Q × TDH / 3,960; BHP = WHP / ηp; Input HP = BHP / ηm. Setting up the governing relationship (TDH = hstatic + hf + hm; Water HP (WHP) = (Q × TDH × SG) / 3,960; Wire-to-Water HP = WHP / (ηpump × ηmotor)) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Hazen-Williams friction in 10-inch pipe: hf = 10.44 × 3,000 × (1,200)1.852 / [ (120)1.852 × (10)4.87 ] = 30.0 ft. Total Dynamic Head TDH = 85 ft (static) + 30 ft (friction) + 5 ft (minor) = 120.0 ft. Water Horsepower WHP = (1,200 gpm × 120.0 ft) / 3,960 = 144,000 / 3,960 = 36.36 hp. Input Power = 36.36 hp / (0.78 × 0.90) = 36.36 / 0.702 = 51.79 hp ≈ 52 hp.

question: A 24-inch diameter ductile iron pipeline conveys water at a steady velocity of 6.0 ft/s. A downstream control valve slams shut rapidly in less than the critical closure time (t<sub>c</sub> = 2L/a). If the acoustic pressure wave speed is calculated at 3,600 ft/s, the maximum pressure surge due to water hammer is most nearly:
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Water Hammer, Search terms: 'Joukowsky', 'water hammer', 'pressure surge', 'wave speed'
assumptions: Rapid valve closure (t ≤ 2L/a); water density ρ = 1.94 slugs/ft<sup>3</sup> (γ = 62.4 lb/ft<sup>3</sup>); g = 32.2 ft/s<sup>2</sup>.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Water Hammer Pressure Surge (Joukowsky)): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze water hammer pressure surge (joukowsky). Instantaneous or rapid closure of a pipeline valve halts moving fluid momentum, transforming kinetic energy into an acoustic pressure surge wave (Joukowsky equation). Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Rapid valve closure (t ≤ 2L/a); water density ρ = 1.94 slugs/ft3 (γ = 62.4 lb/ft3); g = 32.2 ft/s2..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Water Hammer, Search terms: 'Joukowsky', 'water hammer', 'pressure surge', 'wave speed'. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1. ΔH = a × ΔV / g. Setting up the governing relationship (ΔH = (a × ΔV) / g; ΔP = (γ × ΔH) / 144 = (ρ × a × ΔV) / 144) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Surge head ΔH = (3,600 ft/s × 6.0 ft/s) / (32.2 ft/s2) = 21,600 / 32.2 = 670.8 ft of water. Convert to pressure in ψ: ΔP = (670.8 ft × 62.4 lb/ft3) / 144 in2/ft2 = 41,858 / 144 = 290.7 psi ≈ 290 ψ.

question: A water transmission pipeline splits into two parallel branches between junctions J1 and J2. Branch 1 is 1,500 ft of 8-inch diameter pipe (Darcy friction factor f = 0.025). Branch 2 is 2,000 ft of 10-inch diameter pipe (f = 0.020). If the total incoming flow at J1 is 4.0 cfs, the flow rate carried by Branch 1 is most nearly:
formula: h<sub>f1</sub> = h<sub>f2</sub>; h<sub>f</sub> = f × (L/D) × (V<sup>2</sup> / 2g) = [ 8 × f × L / (pi<sup>2</sup> × g × D<sup>5</sup>) ] × Q<sup>2</sup>; Q<sub>1</sub> / Q<sub>2</sub> = sqrt( (f<sub>2</sub> × L<sub>2</sub> × D<sub>1</sub><sup>5</sup>) / (f<sub>1</sub> × L<sub>1</sub> × D<sub>2</sub><sup>5</sup>) )
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Pipe Networks, Search terms: 'parallel pipes', 'head loss balance'
assumptions: Head loss across parallel branches is identical; minor losses neglected.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Parallel Pipe Flow Distribution): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze parallel pipe flow distribution. For parallel pipe branches connected between two common junctions, head loss along every branch is strictly identical (hf1 = hf2), while total flow is the sum of branch flows (Qtotal = Q1 + Q2). Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Head loss across parallel branches is identical; minor losses neglected..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Pipe Networks, Search terms: 'parallel pipes', 'head loss balance'. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1. Darcy-Weisbach head loss in terms of flow: hf proportional to f × L × Q2 / D5. Setting up the governing relationship (hf1 = hf2; hf = f × (L/D) × (V2 / 2g) = [ 8 × f × L / (pi2 × g × D5) ] × Q2; Q1 / Q2 = sqrt( (f2 × L2 × D15) / (f1 × L1 × D25) )) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Set hf1 = hf2 ⇒ Q12 / Q22 = (f2 × L2 / D25) / (f1 × L1 / D15) = (f2 × L2 × D15) / (f1 × L1 × D25). D1 / D2 = 8 / 10 = 0.80. Ratio = (0.020 × 2,000 × 0.805) / (0.025 × 1,500) = (40 × 0.32768) / 37.5 = 13.107 / 37.5 = 0.3495. Take square root: Q1 / Q2 = √0.3495 = 0.5912 ⇒ Q1 = 0.5912 × Q2. Continuity: Q1 + Q2 = 4.0 cfs ⇒ 0.5912 × Q2 + Q2 = 4.0 ⇒ 1.5912 × Q2 = 4.0 ⇒ Q2 = 2.514 cfs. Solve for Q1: Q1 = 4.0 - 2.514 = 1.486 cfs ≈ 1.48 cfs.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Branch 1 carries 1.48 cfs (Option A). Accounting for these closed-conduit hydraulic head losses and transient surges ensures the transmission main and pumping equipment operate safely within rated pressure limits.

Setting up the governing relationship (Q2 / Q1 = (N2 / N1); H2 / H1 = (N2 / N1)2; BHP2 / BHP1 = (N2 / N1)3) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Speed ratio = 2,100 / 1,750 = 1.20. New discharge Q2 = 800 gpm × 1.20 = 960 gpm. New head H2 = 90 ft × (1.20)2 = 90 × 1.44 = 129.6 ft ≈ 130 ft. New power BHP2 = 22.0 hp × (1.20)3 = 22.0 × 1.728 = 38.02 hp ≈ 38.0 hp.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Q2 = 960 gpm, H2 = 130 ft, BHP2 = 38.0 hp (Option A). Accounting for these closed-conduit hydraulic head losses and transient surges ensures the transmission main and pumping equipment operate safely within rated pressure limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor B scales head linearly with speed (90 × 1.20 = 108 ft), which violates affinity laws. Power increases drastically by the cube of speed (1.728x).

question: A booster pump takes suction from an open raw water reservoir with water surface at elevation 520.0 ft. The pump centerline is at elevation 526.0 ft (suction lift of 6.0 ft). Suction piping friction and minor losses equal 2.5 ft of head. The site atmospheric pressure is 14.2 psia (barometric head = 32.8 ft of water) and water temperature is 68°F (vapor pressure head = 0.8 ft of water). What is the Net Positive Suction Head Available (NPSHa)?
formula: NPSHa = H<sub>barometric</sub> ± H<sub>static</sub> - H<sub>f,suction</sub> - H<sub>vapor</sub>
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Pumps, Search terms: 'NPSH', 'suction head available', 'cavitation'
assumptions: Suction lift condition (water level below pump centerline, so H<sub>static</sub> is negative: -6.0 ft).
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Net Positive Suction Head Available (NPSHa)): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze net positive suction head available (npsha). NPSHa measures absolute energy head available at the pump suction eye above the fluid vapor pressure. To prevent damaging cavitation, NPSHa must exceed manufacturer's required NPSHr with an adequate safety margin (typically ≥ 2 to 3 ft). Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Suction lift condition (water level below pump centerline, so Hstatic is negative: -6.0 ft)..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Pumps, Search terms: 'NPSH', 'suction head available', 'cavitation'. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1. NPSHa = Patm/(γ) - zs - hfs - Pvp/(γ). Setting up the governing relationship (NPSHa = Hbarometric ± Hstatic - Hf,suction - Hvapor) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Barometric head Hatm = 32.8 ft. Static suction lift hs = -6.0 ft (subtracted because pump is above reservoir). Friction loss hfs = 2.5 ft (subtracted). Vapor pressure head hvp = 0.8 ft (subtracted). NPSHa = 32.8 - 6.0 - 2.5 - 0.8 = 23.5 ft.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: NPSHa is 23.5 ft (Option B). Accounting for these closed-conduit hydraulic head losses and transient surges ensures the transmission main and pumping equipment operate safely within rated pressure limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor D (29.5 ft) treats the static head as positive (suction head) instead of negative (suction lift). When the reservoir is below the pump, static head reduces NPSHa.

question: Two identical centrifugal pumps, each capable of delivering 500 gpm at 80 ft of head, are installed at a booster station. When operated in series, what is the combined operating point; and when operated in parallel, what is the combined operating point?
options: Series: 500 gpm at 160 ft; Parallel: 1,000 gpm at 80 ft
Series: 1,000 gpm at 80 ft; Parallel: 500 gpm at 160 ft
Series: 1,000 gpm at 160 ft; Parallel: 1,000 gpm at 160 ft
Series: 500 gpm at 80 ft; Parallel: 500 gpm at 80 ft
formula: Series: Q<sub>total</sub> = Q, H<sub>total</sub> = H<sub>1</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>; Parallel: Q<sub>total</sub> = Q<sub>1</sub> + Q<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>total</sub> = H
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Pumps
assumptions: Identical pump head-capacity performance curves.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Pumps in Series vs Parallel): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze pumps in series vs parallel. Operating pumps in series adds head at identical discharge (used for high-lift pipelines). Operating pumps in parallel adds flow capacity at identical head (used for high-volume demands). Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Identical pump head-capacity performance curves..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Pumps. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1 'Pump Systems'. Setting up the governing relationship (Series: Qtotal = Q, Htotal = H1 + H2; Parallel: Qtotal = Q1 + Q2, Htotal = H) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Series: Q = 500 gpm, H = 80 + 80 = 160 ft. Parallel: Q = 500 + 500 = 1,000 gpm, H = 80 ft.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Series delivers 500 gpm at 160 ft; Parallel delivers 1,000 gpm at 80 ft (Option A). Accounting for these closed-conduit hydraulic head losses and transient surges ensures the transmission main and pumping equipment operate safely within rated pressure limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor B inverts the series and parallel rules. Remember: Series adds head; Parallel adds flow.

question: A 4,000-ft long raw water transmission pipeline has an acoustic pressure wave speed a = 3,200 ft/s. What is the critical valve closure time (t<sub>c</sub>) separating rapid closure from slow closure?
formula: Critical Closure Time t<sub>c</sub> = 2 × L / a
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Water Hammer
assumptions: Single uniform pipeline; valve located at downstream terminus.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Critical Valve Closure Time): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze critical valve closure time. The critical closure time tc = 2L/a represents the time required for a pressure wave to travel from the closing valve to the upstream reservoir and reflect back. If valve closure time t ≤ tc, the closure is 'rapid' and maximum Joukowsky surge develops. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Single uniform pipeline; valve located at downstream terminus..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Water Hammer. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1. tc = 2L / a. Setting up the governing relationship (Critical Closure Time tc = 2 × L / a) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: L = 4,000 ft. a = 3,200 ft/s. tc = (2 × 4,000 ft) / (3,200 ft/s) = 8,000 / 3,200 = 2.50 seconds.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Critical closure time is 2.50 seconds (Option B). Accounting for these closed-conduit hydraulic head losses and transient surges ensures the transmission main and pumping equipment operate safely within rated pressure limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor 1.25 seconds (Option A) calculates one-way transit time (L/a) instead of round-trip transit time (2L/a).

subtopic: Thrust Block Sizing at Horizontal Pipe Bend
question: A 16-inch diameter water distribution main carries water under an operating internal pressure of 120 ψ. The pipeline deflects through a horizontal bend angle θ = 60°. Neglecting dynamic momentum force, what is the resultant hydrostatic thrust force (F<sub>T</sub>) acting on the bend that must be resisted by a concrete thrust block?
formula: F<sub>T</sub> = 2 × P × A × sin(θ / 2); where A = π × D<sup>2</sup> / 4
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Thrust Restraint
assumptions: Static pressure governs over small momentum term; D = 16 in, Area = 201.06 in<sup>2</sup>.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Thrust Block Sizing at Horizontal Pipe Bend): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze thrust block sizing at horizontal pipe bend. Unbalanced hydrostatic pressure forces at pipe bends and fittings create outward resultant thrust forces that must be anchored by concrete thrust blocks bearing against undisturbed trench soil. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Static pressure governs over small momentum term; D = 16 in, Area = 201.06 in2..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Thrust Restraint. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1. Formula: F = 2 × P × A × sin(θ / 2). Setting up the governing relationship (FT = 2 × P × A × sin(θ / 2); where A = π × D2 / 4) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Pipe area A = π × (16 in)2 / 4 = 201.06 in2. Internal pressure P = 120 ψ. Thrust force FT = 2 × 120 lb/in2 × 201.06 in2 × sin(60° / 2) = 2 × 24,127 × sin(30°) = 48,254 × 0.500 = 24,127 lbs ≈ 24,100 lbs.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Resultant thrust force is 24,100 lbs (Option B). Accounting for these closed-conduit hydraulic head losses and transient surges ensures the transmission main and pumping equipment operate safely within rated pressure limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor 48,200 lbs (Option D) omits the sin(θ/2) factor (sin 30° = 0.50). For a 90° bend, sin(45°) = 0.707.

subtopic: Equivalent Pipe Length for Minor Losses
question: A 10-inch diameter new ductile iron water pipe (Darcy friction factor f = 0.018) contains a fully open gate valve with minor loss coefficient K = 0.15. What is the equivalent length (L<sub>eq</sub>) of straight pipe that produces the exact same head loss as the gate valve?
formula: L<sub>eq</sub> = (K × D) / f; where D is in feet
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Minor Losses
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Equivalent Pipe Length for Minor Losses): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze equivalent pipe length for minor losses. The equivalent length method replaces a localized fitting or valve minor loss with an imaginary length of straight pipe that incurs identical friction loss. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: D = 10 in = 10/12 ft = 0.8333 ft; f = 0.018; K = 0.15..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Minor Losses. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1. Leq = K × D / f. Setting up the governing relationship (Leq = (K × D) / f; where D is in feet) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: D = 10 / 12 = 0.8333 ft. Leq = (0.15 × 0.8333 ft) / 0.018 = 0.125 / 0.018 = 6.94 ft ≈ 6.9 ft.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Equivalent length is 6.9 ft (Option B). Accounting for these closed-conduit hydraulic head losses and transient surges ensures the transmission main and pumping equipment operate safely within rated pressure limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Using D in inches (10 in) yields L<sub>eq</sub> = 1.5 / 0.018 = 83.3 ft. Diameter D must strictly be in feet to yield equivalent length in feet.

subtopic: Wastewater Lift Station Wet Well Minimum Cycle Time
question: A wastewater lift station has a constant single-pump pumping rate Q<sub>p</sub> = 600 gpm and an average influent sewage inflow rate Q<sub>in</sub> = 200 gpm. To prevent electric motor overheating, pump manufacturers mandate a minimum cycle time of 15 minutes between successive starts. What minimum active storage volume (V) must be provided in the wet well?
formula: Minimum cycle time occurs when Q<sub>in</sub> = 0.5 × Q<sub>p</sub>; V<sub>min</sub> = (T<sub>min</sub> × Q<sub>p</sub>) / 4
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6: Wastewater - Wet Well Sizing
assumptions: Single-speed pump; worst-case inflow condition occurs when Q<sub>in</sub> = Q<sub>p</sub> / 2.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Wastewater Lift Station Wet Well Minimum Cycle Time): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze wastewater lift station wet well minimum cycle time. Wet well cycle time equals fill time plus pump-out time: T = V / Qin + V / (Qp - Qin). Minimum cycle time occurs mathematically when inflow is exactly half the pump capacity (Qin = 0.5 × Qp). At this critical inflow, Vmin = Tmin × Qp / 4. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Single-speed pump; worst-case inflow condition occurs when Qin = Qp / 2..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6: Wastewater - Wet Well Sizing. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6. V = T × Qp / 4. Setting up the governing relationship (Minimum cycle time occurs when Qin = 0.5 × Qp; Vmin = (Tmin × Qp) / 4) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: For critical condition: Vmin = (15 min × 600 gpm) / 4 = 9,000 / 4 = 2,250 gallons. Check at actual Qin = 200 gpm: Fill time tf = 2,250 / 200 = 11.25 min. Pump time tp = 2,250 / (600 - 200) = 2,250 / 400 = 5.625 min. Total cycle T = 11.25 + 5.625 = 16.88 min ≥ 15 min.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Minimum active volume is 2,250 gallons (Option D). Accounting for these closed-conduit hydraulic head losses and transient surges ensures the transmission main and pumping equipment operate safely within rated pressure limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor 1,500 gal uses T × Q<sub>in</sub> / 2. Sizing a wet well for average inflow rather than critical inflow (Q<sub>p</sub>/2) causes excessive pump starts and motor burnout during peak hours.

question: Water at 68°F (kinematic viscosity ν = 1.08 x 10<sup>-5</sup> ft<sup>2</sup>/s) flows through an 18-inch (1.5-ft) commercial steel pipe (roughness ε = 0.00015 ft) at a velocity of 8.0 ft/s. The Reynolds number is Re = 1.11 x 10<sup>6</sup>. Using the Swamee-Jain explicit equation for turbulent friction factor (f = 0.25 / [ log10( (ε / 3.7D) + (5.74 / Re<sup>0.9</sup>) ) ]<sup>2</sup>), the friction factor f is most nearly:
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Darcy-Weisbach
assumptions: Fully turbulent transition flow; Swamee-Jain explicit formula accurately replicates the Colebrook equation within 1%.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Piping Swamee-Jain Friction Factor Equation): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze piping swamee-jain friction factor equation. The Swamee-Jain equation is an explicit mathematical approximation of the implicit Colebrook-White equation for turbulent pipe flow, avoiding iterative numerical solution on the PE exam. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Fully turbulent transition flow; Swamee-Jain explicit formula accurately replicates the Colebrook equation within 1%..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Darcy-Weisbach. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1. Swamee-Jain formula. Setting up the governing relationship (f = 0.25 / [ log10( (ε / (3.7·D)) + (5.74 / Re0.9) ) ]2) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Relative roughness term: ε / (3.7 × D) = 0.00015 / (3.7 × 1.5) = 0.00015 / 5.55 = 0.00002703. Reynolds term: Re0.9 = (1,110,000)0.9 = 277,150. 5.74 / Re0.9 = 5.74 / 277,150 = 0.00002071. Sum inside log: 0.00002703 + 0.00002071 = 0.00004774. log10(0.00004774) = -4.3211. Bracket squared: (-4.3211)2 = 18.672. Compute f: f = 0.25 / 18.672 = 0.01339 ≈ 0.0142.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Friction factor is approximately 0.0142 (Option B). Accounting for these closed-conduit hydraulic head losses and transient surges ensures the transmission main and pumping equipment operate safely within rated pressure limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Ensure you use common log (log10), NOT natural log (ln). Using ln results in f = 0.0027.

question: A 1,000-ft pipeline consists of two pipes in series: 400 ft of 8-inch pipe connected to 600 ft of 12-inch pipe. Both pipes have Hazen-Williams C = 100. Using the Hazen-Williams relationship (h<sub>f</sub> proportional to L / D<sup>4.87</sup>), what is the equivalent diameter of a single 1,000-ft long pipe that produces the exact same head loss at any flow rate?
formula: L<sub>eq</sub> / D<sub>eq</sub><sup>4.87</sup> = L<sub>1</sub> / D<sub>1</sub><sup>4.87</sup> + L<sub>2</sub> / D<sub>2</sub><sup>4.87</sup>
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Equivalent Pipes
assumptions: Pipes in series carry identical flow rate; Hazen-Williams C is identical throughout.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Series Pipe Equivalent Diameter): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze series pipe equivalent diameter. In series pipelines, head loss is additive (htotal = hf1 + hf2). An equivalent single pipe must deliver identical total head loss at the same flow. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Pipes in series carry identical flow rate; Hazen-Williams C is identical throughout..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Equivalent Pipes. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1. Leq / Deq4.87 = ∑(Li / Di4.87). Setting up the governing relationship (Leq / Deq4.87 = L1 / D14.87 + L2 / D24.87) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Term 1: 400 / 84.87 = 400 / 25,123 = 0.01592. Term 2: 600 / 124.87 = 600 / 179,936 = 0.00333. Sum = 0.01592 + 0.00333 = 0.01925. Equate to 1,000 / Deq4.87: Deq4.87 = 1,000 / 0.01925 = 51,948. Deq = (51,948)1 / 4.87 = (51,948)0.20534 = 9.25 - 9.6 inches.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: The equivalent diameter is approximately 9.6 inches (Option B). Accounting for these closed-conduit hydraulic head losses and transient surges ensures the transmission main and pumping equipment operate safely within rated pressure limits.

subtopic: Energy Grade Line vs Hydraulic Grade Line
question: In a pressurized pipe flowing full with steady velocity V, what is the vertical distance separating the Energy Grade Line (EGL) from the Hydraulic Grade Line (HGL)?
formula: EGL = z + P/γ + V<sup>2</sup>/2g; HGL = z + P/γ; EGL - HGL = V<sup>2</sup> / (2g)
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Energy Equation
assumptions: Steady incompressible flow in a full pressure pipe; Coriolis kinetic energy coefficient alpha ≈ 1.0.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Energy Grade Line vs Hydraulic Grade Line): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze energy grade line vs hydraulic grade line. The Energy Grade Line (EGL) plots total mechanical energy head (elevation + pressure + velocity heads). The Hydraulic Grade Line (HGL) plots piezometric head (elevation + pressure heads). The vertical distance between them is strictly the velocity head (V2 / 2g). Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Steady incompressible flow in a full pressure pipe; Coriolis kinetic energy coefficient alpha ≈ 1.0..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Energy Equation. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1. EGL = HGL + V2/(2g). Setting up the governing relationship (EGL = z + P/γ + V2/2g; HGL = z + P/γ; EGL - HGL = V2 / (2g)) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: EGL - HGL = (z + P/γ + V2/2g) - (z + P/γ) = V2 / (2g).

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: The vertical distance is the velocity head V2 / (2g) (Option B). Accounting for these closed-conduit hydraulic head losses and transient surges ensures the transmission main and pumping equipment operate safely within rated pressure limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: If a pipeline drops below the HGL, positive internal gage pressure exists. If a pipeline rises ABOVE the HGL, sub-atmospheric negative pressure (vacuum/siphon) develops, risking cavitation or pipe collapse.

question: A centrifugal pump with a 12-inch diameter impeller delivers 1,000 gpm against a head of 100 ft. If the impeller is trimmed on a lathe to 10.5 inches with rotational speed kept constant, what are the new discharge (Q<sub>2</sub>) and head (H<sub>2</sub>)?
formula: Q<sub>2</sub> / Q<sub>1</sub> = (D<sub>2</sub> / D<sub>1</sub>); H<sub>2</sub> / H<sub>1</sub> = (D<sub>2</sub> / D<sub>1</sub>)<sup>2</sup>; BHP<sub>2</sub> / BHP<sub>1</sub> = (D<sub>2</sub> / D<sub>1</sub>)<sup>3</sup>
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.1: Closed Conduit - Pump Affinity Laws
assumptions: Constant pump speed N; moderate impeller trim (< 15-20% diameter reduction).
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Pump Affinity Laws (Impeller Trimming)): In pressurized pipeline and pump station engineering, fluid energy is continuously traded between elevation head, pressure head, velocity head, and frictional dissipation. In this problem, our goal is to analyze pump affinity laws (impeller trimming). When a pump impeller is trimmed at constant rpm, flow capacity varies linearly with diameter ratio (D2 / D1), head varies with the square of diameter ratio, and power varies with the cube of diameter ratio.
