subtopic: Secondary Clarifier Solids Flux Analysis & Limiting Flux
question: A secondary clarifier operates at an influent flow Q = 4.0 MGD, return sludge flow Q<sub>r</sub> = 1.50 MGD, and MLSS = 3,000 mg/L. Clarifier surface area is A = 7,000 ft<sup>2</sup>. Batch settling tests yield a settling velocity curve where the gravity solids flux reaches a minimum. If the limiting solids flux is determined to be G<sub>L</sub> = 22.0 lb/(ft<sup>2</sup> · day), what is the actual operating solids loading rate (SLR), and is the clarifier safe against thickening overload?
formula: SLR = (Q + Qr) × MLSS × 8.34A; Safe if SLR ≤ GL
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4: Wastewater - Solids Flux
assumptions: Secondary clarifier solids mass includes both forward plant flow Q and recycle flow Q<sub>r.</sub>
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Secondary Clarifier Solids Flux Analysis & Limiting Flux): In municipal wastewater collection and biological treatment, engineers balance hydraulic conveyance with microbial kinetics to remove organic carbon, nutrients, and suspended solids. In this problem, our goal is to analyze secondary clarifier solids flux analysis & limiting flux. Secondary clarifier failure occurs when the applied solids loading rate exceeds the limiting solids flux GL determined from the batch settling curve, causing sludge blanket buildup and solids washout in the effluent. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Secondary clarifier solids mass includes both forward plant flow Q and recycle flow Qr..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4: Wastewater - Solids Flux. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4 'Solids Flux Analysis'. Setting up the governing relationship (SLR = (Q + Qr) × MLSS × 8.34A; Safe if SLR ≤ GL) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Total hydraulic flow entering clarifier = 4.0 + 1.50 = 5.50 MGD. Total applied solids mass = 5.50 MGD × 3,000 mg/L × 8.34 = 137,610 lb solids/day. Applied solids loading rate SLR = 137,610 lb/day7,000 ft2 = 19.659 lb/(ft2 · day) ≈ 19.7 lb/(ft2 · day). Compare to limiting flux: SLR = 19.7 < GL = 22.0 lb/(ft2 · day).

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: SLR = 19.7 lb/(ft2 · day), which is safe (Option B). Maintaining this operational parameter keeps the biological treatment process stable and ensures the plant reliably meets its NPDES effluent discharge permit limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor 14.3 lb/(ft<sup>2.</sup>day) omits the return activated sludge flow Q<sub>r</sub> (using only 4.0 MGD). Secondary clarifiers must ALWAYS include Q<sub>r</sub> for solids loading.

subtopic: Anaerobic Digestion Volatile Solids Reduction (Van Kleeck Formula)
question: A complete-mix anaerobic digester operates at 35°C. Raw sludge fed to the digester has a total volatile solids content of Vin = 72.0% of total solids (0.720). Digested sludge withdrawn has a volatile solids content of Vout = 52.0% (0.520). Using the standard Van Kleeck formula VSR = Vin - VoutVin - (Vin · Vout) × 100%, what is the percent Volatile Solids Reduction (VSR)?
formula: VSR (%) = Vin - VoutVin - (Vin · Vout) × 100%
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4: Wastewater - Sludge Digestion
assumptions: Fixed (ash) solids remain constant and conservative through anaerobic digestion.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Anaerobic Digestion Volatile Solids Reduction (Van Kleeck Formula)): In municipal wastewater collection and biological treatment, engineers balance hydraulic conveyance with microbial kinetics to remove organic carbon, nutrients, and suspended solids. In this problem, our goal is to analyze anaerobic digestion volatile solids reduction (van kleeck formula). Fixed mineral ash solids do not degrade during digestion. The Van Kleeck formula uses fixed solids as an internal tracer to calculate true fractional volatile solids destruction. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Fixed (ash) solids remain constant and conservative through anaerobic digestion..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4: Wastewater - Sludge Digestion. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4 'Van Kleeck Equation'. Setting up the governing relationship (VSR (%) = Vin - VoutVin - (Vin · Vout) × 100%) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Numerator = Vin - Vout = 0.720 - 0.520 = 0.200. Product Vin · Vout = 0.720 × 0.520 = 0.3744. Denominator = 0.720 - 0.3744 = 0.3456. Compute VSR: VSR = 0.2000.3456 × 100% = 57.87% ≈ 57.9%.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Volatile solids reduction is 57.9% (Option D). Maintaining this operational parameter keeps the biological treatment process stable and ensures the plant reliably meets its NPDES effluent discharge permit limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor 27.8% simply computes (0.72 - 0.52)/0.72 = 27.8%, which ignores the changing total mass basis. Van Kleeck's formula is mandatory on the PE exam.

subtopic: Anaerobic Digester Methane Gas Production & Energy Yield
question: An anaerobic digester destroys 6,000 lb of volatile solids per day. Standard digestion gas production yields 15.0 ft<sup>3</sup> of biogas per pound of VS destroyed, with a volumetric methane content of 65.0% CH<sub>4</sub> (methane lower heating value = 990 BTU/ft<sup>3</sup>). If a combined heat and power (CHP) engine operates with a thermal conversion efficiency of 40.0%, what is the daily recovered thermal heating output in million BTUs (MMBTU/day)?
formula: Biogas (ft<sup>3</sup>/day) = VS Destroyed × 15.0; CH<sub>4</sub> Volume = Biogas × 0.65; Energy = CH<sub>4</sub> × 990 × η
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4: Wastewater - Sludge Digestion
assumptions: Standard mesophilic biogas yield: 15 ft<sup>3</sup>/lb VS destroyed; methane heating value = 990 BTU/ft<sup>3</sup>.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Anaerobic Digester Methane Gas Production & Energy Yield): In municipal wastewater collection and biological treatment, engineers balance hydraulic conveyance with microbial kinetics to remove organic carbon, nutrients, and suspended solids. In this problem, our goal is to analyze anaerobic digester methane gas production & energy yield. Anaerobic methanogenesis converts destroyed volatile fatty acids into methane and carbon dioxide biogas. Recovered energy depends on methane fraction and engine thermal heat exchanger efficiency. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Standard mesophilic biogas yield: 15 ft3/lb VS destroyed; methane heating value = 990 BTU/ft3..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4: Wastewater - Sludge Digestion. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4. Digester gas energy calculations. Setting up the governing relationship (Biogas (ft3/day) = VS Destroyed × 15.0; CH4 Volume = Biogas × 0.65; Energy = CH4 × 990 × η) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Total daily biogas = 6,000 lb VS/day × 15.0 ft3/lb = 90,000 ft3 biogas/day. Daily methane volume = 90,000 × 0.65 = 58,500 ft3 CH4/day. Total combustion heat = 58,500 ft3 × 990 BTU/ft3 = 57,915,000 BTU/day = 57.915 MMBTU/day. Recovered thermal output (40%) = 57.915 × 0.40 = 23.166 MMBTU/day ≈ 23.2 MMBTU/day.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Recovered thermal energy is 23.2 MMBTU/day (Option A). Maintaining this operational parameter keeps the biological treatment process stable and ensures the plant reliably meets its NPDES effluent discharge permit limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor 57.9 MMBTU/day is the total unrecovered fuel heating value without applying the 40% thermal heat recovery efficiency.

question: A gravity sludge thickener receives 12,000 gallons/day of waste activated sludge at a solids concentration of 1.0% (99.0% moisture, P<sub>1</sub> = 99.0). Thickened sludge underflow achieves a solids concentration of 4.0% (96.0% moisture, P<sub>2</sub> = 96.0). Assuming zero solids loss in the supernatant, what is the daily volume of thickened sludge (V<sub>2</sub>)?
formula: V1(100 - P1) = V2(100 - P2) ⇒ V2 = V1 × %solids1%solids2
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4: Wastewater - Sludge Thickening
assumptions: 100% solids capture; specific gravity ≈ 1.00.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Sludge Volume Thickening & Moisture Reduction): In municipal wastewater collection and biological treatment, engineers balance hydraulic conveyance with microbial kinetics to remove organic carbon, nutrients, and suspended solids. In this problem, our goal is to analyze sludge volume thickening & moisture reduction. Because water is removed during thickening while dry solids mass remains constant, sludge volume is inversely proportional to solids concentration: V1 × S1 = V2 × S2. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: 100% solids capture; specific gravity ≈ 1.00..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4: Wastewater - Sludge Thickening. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4 'Sludge Thickening'. Setting up the governing relationship (V1(100 - P1) = V2(100 - P2) ⇒ V2 = V1 × %solids1%solids2) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Initial solids content = 1.0%. Thickened solids content = 4.0%. Volume relation: 12,000 gal/day × 1.0% = V2 × 4.0% ⇒ V2 = 12,000 × 1.04.0 = 3,000 gal/day.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Thickened sludge volume is 3,000 gal/day (Option A). Maintaining this operational parameter keeps the biological treatment process stable and ensures the plant reliably meets its NPDES effluent discharge permit limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Increasing solids concentration from 1% to 4% reduces total liquid volume by a massive 75% (from 12,000 to 3,000 gal/day), dramatically downsizing downstream digesters.

subtopic: Belt Filter Press Dewatering & Polymer Conditioning
question: A belt filter press dewaters 20.0 dry tons of digested sludge per day (40,000 lb dry solids/day). The sludge feed is conditioned with an active dry polymer dosage of 14.0 lb polymer per dry ton of sludge. Liquid emulsion polymer is supplied at 40.0% active polymer content with specific gravity 1.08. The dewatered sludge cake produces 22.0% solids. What is the daily consumption of commercial liquid polymer in gallons per day, and what total weight of wet sludge cake (in wet tons/day) is hauled to disposal?
formula: Polymer (lb/day) = Dry Tons × Dose(lb/ton); Polymer (gpd) = Polymer lbSs × 8.34 × %active; Wet Cake = Dry Tons%cake solids
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.4: Wastewater - Sludge Dewatering
assumptions: 100% solids capture; 1 ton = 2,000 lbs.
steps: 1. In this problem, our goal is to analyze belt filter press dewatering & polymer conditioning. Sludge conditioning destabilizes colloidal repulsive charges before mechanical squeezing on a belt filter press. Haul weight depends directly on final dewatered cake solids fraction. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: 100% solids capture; 1 ton = 2,000 lbs..

Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Total dry polymer required = 20.0 dry tons/day × 14.0 lb/ton = 280.0 lb active polymer/day. question: A wastewater treatment plant discharges 8.0 MGD of secondary effluent into a trout stream with a strict permit limit of zero detectable chlorine residual. Following chlorine contact, the effluent contains a total residual chlorine of 1.80 mg/L. Sodium bisulfite (NaHSO<sub>3</sub>) is dosed for dechlorination: NaHSO<sub>3</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2O</sub> → NaHSO<sub>4</sub> + 2 HCl, with a stoichiometric ratio of 1.465 lb pure NaHSO<sub>3</sub> per lb Cl<sub>2.</sub> Applying a 15.0% operational excess safety margin, how many pounds of pure sodium bisulfite must be fed per day?
formula: Chlorine Mass (lb/day) = Q(MGD) × [Cl<sub>2</sub>](mg/L) × 8.34; Bisulfite Mass = Chlorine Mass × 1.465 × (1 + Excess)
reference: NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.3: Wastewater - Dechlorination
assumptions: Stoichiometric reaction: 1.465 lb NaHSO<sub>3</sub> per lb Cl<sub>2</sub>; 15% excess over stoichiometric.
steps: 1. The Engineering Story & Problem Setup (Effluent Dechlorination Stoichiometry (Sulfur Dioxide / Bisulfite)): In municipal wastewater collection and biological treatment, engineers balance hydraulic conveyance with microbial kinetics to remove organic carbon, nutrients, and suspended solids. In this problem, our goal is to analyze effluent dechlorination stoichiometry (sulfur dioxide / bisulfite). Free and combined chlorine residuals are highly toxic to aquatic life. Dechlorination chemicals (sodium bisulfite or sulfur dioxide) rapidly reduce residual chlorine to inert chloride ions. Before plugging in numbers, we set up our system boundary under the engineering assumptions: Stoichiometric reaction: 1.465 lb NaHSO3 per lb Cl2; 15% excess over stoichiometric..

2. How to Set Up the Equation (NCEES Handbook v2.2 Strategy): On the CBT exam, open your NCEES Reference Handbook v2.2 to NCEES PE Civil Reference Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.3: Wastewater - Dechlorination. NCEES Handbook v2.2, Section 4.6.3 'Dechlorination'. Setting up the governing relationship (Chlorine Mass (lb/day) = Q(MGD) × [Cl2](mg/L) × 8.34; Bisulfite Mass = Chlorine Mass × 1.465 × (1 + Excess)) lets us isolate the target unknown directly in terms of the given field measurements.

3. Step-by-Step Mathematical Walkthrough & Unit Consistency: Now let's walk through the numbers step by step, making sure all units are dimensionally consistent before solving: Total residual chlorine mass = 8.0 MGD × 1.80 mg/L × 8.34 (lb/MG)/(mg/L) = 120.096 lb Cl2/day. Stoichiometric bisulfite needed = 120.096 lb Cl2/day × 1.465 lb NaHSO3/lb Cl2 = 175.94 lb/day. Applying 15% excess safety factor: 175.94 × 1.15 = 202.33 lb/day ≈ 202 lb/day.

4. Engineering Conclusion & Field Sanity Check: Required sodium bisulfite is 202 lb/day (Option C). Maintaining this operational parameter keeps the biological treatment process stable and ensures the plant reliably meets its NPDES effluent discharge permit limits.
pitfall: Exam Day Trap & Distractor Analysis: Distractor 120 lb/day is the mass of chlorine alone. Distractor 176 lb/day is stoichiometric bisulfite without the 15% operational safety margin.
